The last X-10 flew on 26 January 1959 and crashed about fifty-seven miles downrange after a power failure. The disposition of the airframes follows [North American X-10][ref_x10], and the target flights follow [Cleary 1991 The 6555th, The NAVAHO Program][ref_cleary_1991].

The programme therefore divides into three phases with different purposes. The Edwards phase from October 1953 established that the vehicle flew and could be recovered. The Cape phase from August 1955 extended the envelope and flew the navigation legs. The five dedicated autonavigator flights in that phase are the only part of the programme that addressed the keystone question directly. The post-cancellation phase from September 1958 used surplus airframes as targets for a different programme entirely. Remaining hardware from a cancelled programme ordinarily ends this way, and the phase tells nothing about the vehicle.

### What Was Demonstrated

Stating the achievements precisely matters because the article's argument is that the vehicle worked and the test did not. The X-10 reached Mach 2.05, which is above the free-flight model's tested maximum of 1.70 and therefore beyond where either ground method had been validated. It reached 49,000 feet in [North American X-10][ref_x10] and 44,800 feet in [Jenkins Landis and Miller 2003 American X-Vehicles, An Inventory X-1 to X-50][book_jenkins_landis_miller_2003]. It flew about a thousand kilometres in a single flight. It took off and landed under automatic control on a runway. Considered as an aeroplane, and particularly as an unmanned aeroplane in 1955, this is an impressive record, and [Parsch 2002 RTV-A-5 X-10][ref_parsch_x10] records that for a short time it was the fastest turbojet-powered aircraft flown.

None of it bears on why the record leaves the programme's question open. **A vehicle can be flown perfectly and still fail to constitute an experiment.** The identifiability calculation above shows that window length was no obstacle on the one navigation flight whose duration is reported, so the weakness lies in how few navigator flights were completed, two of the five having been aborted. The X-10's sorties were successful flights and too few measurements, and those are independent properties.

### The Dive Flights as a Test of the Terminal Phase

Three vehicles flown at the Cape were expended in planned dives against Grand Bahama Island, and these are usually listed alongside the accidental losses as though they were the same kind of event. They were not. The Navaho's terminal phase was a dive onto the target from cruise altitude, and the Air Force history [Landis 2020 Flashback, The Navaho Missile, Part 1][ref_landis_2020_part_1] lists dive technique among the things the Cape flights were to check. A dive from twenty-four kilometres at Mach three is a distinct flight condition, with its own structural loads, control problem, and contribution to the accuracy budget. **A vehicle that navigates perfectly and then misses the dive has still missed.** The sensitivity is easy to state. A dive from altitude $h$ at flight path angle $\gamma$ covers a ground range of

$$x = \frac{h}{\tan \gamma}$$

so an error in the dive angle produces a range error of

$$\frac{dx}{d\gamma} = -\frac{h}{\sin^{2} \gamma}$$

and from twenty-four kilometres at forty-five degrees this is

$$\frac{dx}{d\gamma} = -\frac{24{,}000}{0.5} = -48{,}000 \, \text{m/rad}$$

or **48 metres of miss for every milliradian of dive-angle error**. Against an eight-hundred-metre requirement that is a demanding pointing accuracy, separate from knowing where the target is. Expending three airframes to fly that phase deliberately is therefore a test decision rather than a disposal, and is evidence that the programme understood the terminal phase as a distinct problem even though the X-10 could only approximate its conditions. [Wheeler 1946][research_wheeler_1946] treats the assessment of where a weapon landed, the measurement such a flight exists to produce. The terminal-guidance alternative of looking at the target on the way down is [Dunmire and Lopresti 1963][research_dunmire_lopresti_1963], the accuracy requirement that a re-entering body imposes on its guidance is [Broglio 1961][research_broglio_1961], and what happens on arrival is [Johnson and Mosely 1964][research_johnson_mosely_1964].

### What the Losses Say

Stated as a fraction, twelve of thirteen vehicles lost is

$$\frac{12}{13} = 0.923$$

and twenty-seven development flights across thirteen airframes is 2.08 flights per vehicle. **A design whose entire economic and statistical rationale was repeated use averaged two flights per article.** The causes named for the landing losses at the Cape are concentrated at the end of the mission rather than in it, with vehicles that veered off the strip, drag chutes that did not deploy, and barriers that were not engaged, as [Parsch 2002 RTV-A-5 X-10][ref_parsch_x10] lists them. The vehicle flew supersonically and navigated across a range, and then could not reliably stop.

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

Three levels of evidence exist for this configuration and they can be set against one another. [Pfyl 1952][research_pfyl_1952] gives wind-tunnel data on a 0.07-scale model. [Bond and Swanson 1953][research_bond_swanson_1953] gives free-flight data on a 0.12-scale rocket-boosted model at Reynolds numbers from nine to twenty-four million. The full-scale vehicle flew to Mach 2.05, faster than either model had been tested.

The pattern is familiar from the [X-7][related_post_a304_lockheed_x7]. Free flight extends the Reynolds number far beyond what the tunnels of the period could reach and removes support interference, at the cost of a single trajectory per model and no ability to repeat a condition. The Reynolds numbers make the point concrete. On mean aerodynamic chord,

$$Re = \frac{\rho v \bar{c}}{\mu}$$

and evaluating it for the full-scale vehicle at its ceiling and maximum Mach number, with the viscosity from Sutherland's relation

$$\mu = \frac{1.458 \times 10^{-6} \, T^{3/2}}{T + 110.4} = 1.42 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{Pa s}$$

gives

$$Re_{\text{full}} = \frac{0.2397 \times 604.9 \times 4.595}{1.42 \times 10^{-5}} = 4.68 \times 10^{7}$$

The free-flight models spanned nine to twenty-four million, so they reached

$$\frac{Re_{\text{model}}}{Re_{\text{full}}} = 0.19 \; \text{to} \; 0.51$$

**between a fifth and a half of full-scale Reynolds number**, against transonic tunnels of the period that typically delivered a few million on a model of comparable size. The free-flight technique therefore bought roughly an order of magnitude over the tunnels and still fell short of the vehicle by a factor of two. Stated that way the result is more defensible than a claim that the models reached flight conditions. The technique had already been applied to full-scale guided missiles by [Delsasso et al 1948][research_delsasso_1948], five years before the X-10 flew, so the method was mature even where its Reynolds numbers were not.

Two of the free-flight findings are checkable against the analysis performed here and both survive. The reported drag-rise Mach number near 0.90 is consistent with a thin low-aspect-ratio configuration, and the reported doubling of minimum drag from subsonic to supersonic is what wave drag on such a shape produces. The base-drag finding of twenty-five percent of minimum drag supersonically is large but not anomalous for a configuration with a blunt afterbody carrying two engine exhausts. The duct recovery result illustrates the tension, because the free-flight model's report of recovery below normal-shock values is either a real property of the inlet design or an artefact of a small duct at model scale, and **no measurement in the accessible record distinguishes those two possibilities**. The full-scale vehicle's own inlet performance does not appear in the public literature at all, so the thrust-balance inference above had to be constructed from the vehicle's demonstrated speed instead.

The free-flight technique deserves naming, because it produced the only surviving quantitative data on this configuration. Its development and its limits are [Turner 1965][research_turner_1965], and comparable applications in the same era are [Wetzel 1954][research_wetzel_1954], [Ball and Smith 1956][research_ball_smith_1956], and [Grant and Sevier 1960][research_grant_sevier_1960]. The technique's central bargain can be restated in the terms this article has been using. **A free-flight model gives one trajectory and therefore one sample**, the same difficulty the X-10 had with drift statistics, one level down in scale. A programme that needs a distribution and can afford only single samples is in the same trouble whether the article being flown is a scale model or a full-size vehicle.

## What the Data Changed

### The Cancellation of the Navaho

Air Force Headquarters terminated the Navaho by message dated 12 July 1957. The XSM-64 had flown first on 6 November 1956, and its pitch gyroscope failed ten seconds after lift-off and the vehicle broke up at twenty-six seconds. Three further launches through 26 June 1957 failed in turn, one impacting twenty-five nautical miles downrange, one falling back onto the pad after rising four feet, and one losing its ramjets after booster separation. Seven more tests followed through November 1958 without a full-range success. The launch record is that of [Cleary 1991 The 6555th, The NAVAHO Program][ref_cleary_1991], with the later tests in [Parsch 2002 SM-64][ref_parsch_sm64]. **The X-10 was the most successful part of a programme that failed**, and by the time the vehicle had demonstrated what it could demonstrate, the ballistic alternatives had made the question moot.

The strategic argument is not primarily an engineering one, yet it can be derived rather than asserted. A ballistic missile covering the same ten thousand kilometres flies a minimum-energy ellipse. Writing the range angle as

$$\Phi = \frac{R_{m}}{R_{e}} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{7}}{6.371 \times 10^{6}} = 1.570 \, \text{rad}$$

the minimum-energy condition fixes the burnout speed through

$$\lambda = \frac{V^{2}}{g R_{e}} = \frac{2 \sin (\Phi/2)}{1 + \sin (\Phi/2)} = 0.828$$

giving

$$V = \sqrt{0.828 \times 9.80665 \times 6.371 \times 10^{6}} = 7193 \, \text{m/s}$$

and a semi-major axis from the vis-viva relation of

$$a = \frac{R_{e}}{2 - \lambda} = 5.437 \times 10^{6} \, \text{m}$$

with eccentricity 0.415 and an apogee 1319 kilometres above the surface. Converting the true anomalies at launch and impact to mean anomalies and differencing gives the free-flight time

$$t_{\text{ballistic}} = \frac{\Delta M}{n} = 1932 \, \text{s} = 32.2 \, \text{minutes}$$

against the cruise mission's 172 minutes. The ratio is

$$\frac{t_{\text{cruise}}}{t_{\text{ballistic}}} = \frac{172.2}{32.2} = 5.35$$

**The airbreathing weapon is exposed more than five times as long, and it is exposed inside the atmosphere at twenty-four kilometres where an interceptor can reach it, while its competitor spends most of its flight far above the atmosphere, reaching thirteen hundred kilometres at apogee, where in 1957 nothing could.** The cancellation argument is complete at that point. Once Atlas and Titan were credible, no accuracy improvement available at the time bought enough to pay for a factor of five in exposure against a threat that could not be engaged at all.

The ballistic relations used above are period material and not modern reconstructions. [Wheelon 1959][research_wheelon_1959] treats the free flight of a ballistic missile in the form derived here, [Brooks 1961][research_brooks_1961] gives the basic theory of ballistic missile performance, and [Ostner 1962][research_ostner_1962] reduces it to a program that a range could run. [Schweppe 1964][research_schweppe_1964] estimates where such a body is while it flies. [Faulkner 1961][research_faulkner_1961] poses the interception problem as the period saw it, [Fye 1966][research_fye_1966] states the defensive difficulty plainly, [Kashiwagi 1968][research_kashiwagi_1968] predicts the trajectories being intercepted, and [Werrell 1985 The Evolution of the Cruise Missile][book_werrell_1985] carries the history of the class that lost the argument.

### What Survived

The programme's outputs outlived its purpose in three directions, and the question is which of them the X-10 can claim.

**The engines.** The liquid rocket booster engines developed for the Navaho became the basis of the Rocketdyne line that powered Redstone, Jupiter, Thor, and Atlas, and through Atlas the American space programme, as the [Navaho][ref_navaho] entry summarises. The Redstone half of that inheritance is documented in [Bullard 1965][research_bullard_1965], and a released Rocketdyne sustainer specification of the resulting line is [Scott 1963][research_scott_1963]. This is by a wide margin the largest technical legacy of the Navaho effort. **It belongs entirely to the booster and the X-10 had no part in it whatever**, since the X-10 carried no rocket engine and took off under turbojet power.

**The navigation.** The navigation work is the legacy the X-10 can properly claim, because the X-10 is where the N-6 was first flown in a missile airframe, after aircraft trials described in [Landis 2020 Navaho Missile Program, Part 2][ref_landis_2020_part_2]. The error analysis of that architecture, as the period came to understand it, is [Dusek 1964][research_dusek_1964_2] and [Nash 1968][research_nash_1968]. The guidance system fed forward into nuclear-powered submarines, Navy attack aircraft, and the Hound Dog and Minuteman missiles [Cleary 1991 The 6555th, The NAVAHO Program][ref_cleary_1991], and the combination of a Schuler-tuned platform with an automatic celestial reference remained a standard solution for unaided long-range navigation until satellite navigation displaced it, and has returned to favour as satellite navigation has become contestable.

**The configuration.** Experience with large supersonic canard configurations, with side-mounted supersonic inlets, and with the structures and systems of sustained supersonic flight fed into subsequent work at the same company, most visibly the XB-70, which [Landis 2020 Navaho Missile Program, Part 2][ref_landis_2020_part_2] names among the beneficiaries. The connection is real but diffuse and this article does not attempt to quantify it.

**What the X-10 did not change is the Navaho's outcome.** By the time the vehicle had flown its full programme, the weapon it served had been cancelled, and the cancellation turned on an argument about exposure time that no amount of aerodynamic or navigational success would have answered.

**The X-10's contribution is harder to point at than any of these**, and honesty requires saying so. It demonstrated that a large unmanned supersonic vehicle could be flown repeatedly from a runway and recovered, which is a real result. What it did not do was settle the navigation question it was built to settle, chiefly because too few navigator flights were completed to estimate a drift distribution, as computed above.

### Identifiability as a Later Discipline

The article's identifiability result is that two error signatures are 97.4 percent correlated over a maximum-speed X-10 leg and 14.0 percent correlated over the 79-minute navigation flight, so whether the drift rate could be separated from the accelerometer bias depends on the window actually flown. The result concerns identifiability, which is now a field.

The modern distinction the X-10's difficulty falls under is between structural and practical identifiability. A parameter is structurally identifiable if the model permits it to be recovered from perfect data and practically identifiable if the data actually collected suffice. **The X-10's drift rate was structurally identifiable, and its practical identifiability turned on the window and the number of flights**, the distinction drawn by [Simpson and Baker 2026][research_simpson_baker_2026] and by [Heitzman-Breen et al 2026][research_heitzman_breen_2026], with the structural side treated by [Salmaniw and Browning 2025][research_salmaniw_browning_2025]. [Liu et al 2026][research_liu_2026_2] gives the remedy, choosing the experiment so that the parameter becomes practically identifiable. The Fisher information matrix that quantifies how much an experiment reveals is [Andrade et al 2025][research_andrade_2025] and [Fayette et al 2026][research_fayette_2026], and the input-design problem of exciting a system enough to identify it is [Campregher et al 2025][research_campregher_2025], with parameter subset selection in [Wang and Qi 2024][research_wang_qi_2024].

**The window sweep performed above is an optimal-experiment-design calculation with one free variable**, and the answer it returns, namely a flight of exactly one Schuler period, is the sort of answer that discipline exists to produce. Observability, the closely related property, is now analysed for inertial systems directly in [Yang et al 2026][research_yang_2026_3] and [Zhang et al 2026][research_zhang_2026_2], and observability-driven design of a celestial navigation observation appears in [Hou et al 2025][research_hou_2025].

The 1953 programme had none of this vocabulary. It cannot be charged with ignoring a known method, because the method it needed had not been invented, and the article adopts that reading as the fairest available.

### Inertial Error Propagation by Covariance

The error analysis this article performs by hand is now standard and automated. [Blum and Dambeck 2020][research_blum_dambeck_2020] propagates coloured noise through inertial mechanisations, [Brouk and DeMars 2021][research_brouk_demars_2021] handles uncertainty propagation with conic constraints, and [Bhatia and Geller 2020][research_bhatia_geller_2020] performs sensitivity analysis for precision inertial sensors. The relevant modern point is that the crossover time computed here as a single scalar is now the output of a full covariance propagation, and that the qualitative structure of a bounded accelerometer term against a secular gyroscope term survives unchanged. Theoretical error modelling of a strapdown system in the same tradition is [Mohammadkarimi et al 2025][research_mohammadkarimi_2025_2].

### Alignment and Calibration

The relation derived above puts one arcminute of azimuth misalignment at 2.9 kilometres of cross-track error at intercontinental range, which makes ground alignment a coequal partner of airborne drift rather than a preliminary to it. That problem is still worked. Initial alignment is now attacked with learned models in [Wang et al 2025][research_wang_2025_4], the calibration and compensation of an initial-state error scheme is [Ding et al 2025][research_ding_2025], online calibration by error backpropagation is [Simak et al 2024][research_simak_2024], and Allan-variance-based noise characterisation, the present-day way of asking what an instrument's drift is, appears in [Priya and Deepa 2024][research_priya_deepa_2024], though applied there to a vehicular optical communication link rather than to an inertial instrument.

### Gyroscopes Near the Navaho Requirement

The Navaho needed 0.0025 degrees per hour to meet its early requirement, and the requirement was eventually relaxed to a circular error probable of 12,000 feet after 5,000 miles of flight [Landis 2020 Navaho Missile Program, Part 2][ref_landis_2020_part_2]. Set beside the current literature, the figure gives an unusually exact comparison.

Navigation-grade fibre-optic gyroscopes are [Shang et al 2020][research_shang_2020], [Zhao et al 2022][research_zhao_2022], [Liu et al 2023][research_liu_2023], and [Aleinik et al 2025][research_aleinik_2025]. Micro-electromechanical instruments have closed most of the remaining distance, with [Suzuki et al 2019][research_suzuki_2019] and [Nusbaum et al 2019][research_nusbaum_2019] on the approach, a bias instability of 0.09 degrees per hour in [Wu et al 2021][research_wu_2021], a high-quality-factor hemispherical resonator in [Li et al 2024][research_li_2024], and **a honeycomb disk resonator gyroscope reported at 0.003 degrees per hour in [Chen et al 2025][research_chen_2025]**.

That last figure stands to the Navaho's requirement as

$$\frac{0.003}{0.0025} = 1.20$$

and it is achieved by a micro-electromechanical device. The article's drift relation takes the comparison further than the ratio does. A gyroscope drifting at 0.003 degrees per hour is $1.454 \times 10^{-8}$ radians per second, so over the Navaho mission it would produce

$$\delta x = R_{e} \varepsilon t = 6.371 \times 10^{6} \times 1.454 \times 10^{-8} \times 10{,}333 = 957 \, \text{m}$$

**which still does not meet the eight-hundred-metre requirement on drift alone**, seventy years later and before any of the other budget terms are added. The comparison shows not that the requirement has become easy but that a component, and no longer a national programme, can approach it. The mechanisms that set the floor are now themselves the subject of study, in [Hiller et al 2019][research_hiller_2019] on the origins of bias instability, [Kuang et al 2022][research_kuang_2022] on its temperature dependence, today's version of the platform-oven problem computed above, [Laita et al 2024][research_laita_2024] on nonlinearity, and [Zhao et al 2024][research_zhao_2024] on installation-error propagation. Gyrocompassing, the alignment problem this article showed to be worth 2.9 kilometres per arcminute, is treated afresh in [Bénet and Guinamard 2026][research_benet_guinamard_2026], and the combination of star tracker with gyroscope that the N-6 pioneered is [Zhu et al 2025][research_zhu_2025].

**A requirement that defeated a national weapon programme in 1957 is now nearly met by a component**, and the seventy years between those two statements is the most direct measure available of how far ahead of its instruments the Navaho's accuracy requirement was.

### Star Trackers as Routine Equipment

Automatic celestial reference is now ordinary. [Siemes et al 2019][research_siemes_2019] calibrates a star tracker in orbit, [Ni et al 2019][research_ni_2019] gives attitude-correlated frame methods for weak signals, and [Ning et al 2019][research_ning_2019] integrates star pixel coordinates. The daylight tracking problem the Navaho programme faced is now a design choice rather than a research question.

**The architecture the N-6 pioneered has also come back under its own name.** Stellar-inertial integration is treated directly by [Kondrashkin et al 2025][research_kondrashkin_2025] and by [Yang et al 2026][research_yang_2026], which adds refraction to the celestial observation, and the strapdown version that dispenses with the gimballed platform entirely is [Teague and Chahl 2023][research_teague_chahl_2023] and [Teague and Chahl 2024][research_teague_chahl_2024]. Centroiding accuracy, which sets the arcsecond figure the article inverted from the reported circular error probable, is [Li et al 2023][research_li_2023], the benchmark problem is [Suthakar et al 2026][research_suthakar_2026], delayed measurements in the filter are [Kahraman and Soken 2023][research_kahraman_soken_2023], and the same idea applied on another planet is [Zhan et al 2022][research_zhan_2022], with a deep-space integration in [Wang et al 2024][research_wang_2024].

### Fault Detection

An unmanned vehicle that loses an instrument has no one aboard to notice. The X-10's losses were mostly mechanical and terminal, but the guidance failure mode was live throughout, and [Cleary 1991 The 6555th, The NAVAHO Program][ref_cleary_1991] records that the first XSM-64 launch broke up after its pitch gyroscope failed ten seconds after lift-off. Detecting and identifying such a failure in flight became possible only later, and the founding treatment is [Potter and Deckert 1972][research_potter_deckert_1972], with modern robustness work in [Lee et al 2024][research_lee_2024] and fault-protection architecture in [Schulte and Spencer 2020][research_schulte_spencer_2020]. **The redundancy that would have saved that vehicle was not unavailable for cost reasons. The analytical basis for using it did not yet exist.**

It exists now, and the inertial case is well developed. Fault detection and isolation for redundant inertial measurement units is [Xu et al 2023][research_xu_2023_3] and [Lukoyanov et al 2025][research_lukoyanov_2025], the airborne navigation case is [Dai et al 2023][research_dai_2023], estimation alongside detection is [Huang et al 2023][research_huang_2023], and active fault-tolerant control that reconfigures around a failure rather than merely reporting it is [Zhao et al 2024][research_zhao_2024_2]. **A pitch gyroscope failing ten seconds after lift-off is now a detectable and survivable event.** It is the clearest case in this article of a 1956 loss that modern practice would avoid.

### Navigation Without Satellites

The Navaho's problem was navigating with no external radio reference, and this has become topical again. Terrain-referenced navigation runs through [Park and Park 2019][research_park_park_2019], [Kang et al 2020][research_kang_2020], and [Carroll and Canciani 2021][research_carroll_canciani_2021]. [Zhai and Wang 2020][research_zhai_wang_2020] and [Cui et al 2021][research_cui_2021] filter it robustly, [Alhassan and Ghahremani 2021][research_alhassan_ghahremani_2021] aligns it nonlinearly, and [Ermakov and Gogolev 2021][research_ermakov_gogolev_2021] and [Wang et al 2020][research_wang_2020] compare integration architectures. **The question the X-10 was built to answer is once more an open engineering question**, asked now about vehicles that must operate where satellite navigation is denied.

The breadth of that effort shows how completely satellite navigation had displaced the problem and how completely the displacement has been undone. Visual localisation without satellites is [Shpagin and Panchenko 2026][research_shpagin_panchenko_2026], [Tsiopliakis 2026][research_tsiopliakis_2026], and [Li et al 2026][research_li_2026_4], terrain-relative navigation for descent is reviewed by [Rahuman and Lee 2026][research_rahuman_lee_2026], magnetic anomaly matching, the same trick as gravity matching applied to a different field, is [Pisarski et al 2026][research_pisarski_2026], the underwater case is [Praczyk and Zalewski 2026][research_praczyk_zalewski_2026], and constrained estimation in denied environments is [Yue et al 2026][research_yue_2026]. **Every one of these is a scheme for bounding a secular error with an external observation**, as the star tracker did for the Navaho, and the modern literature has widened the catalogue of things that can serve as the observation.

### Reusability and the Cost of a Sortie

The X-10's economic case for recovery, and its failure to realise that case at 2.08 flights per airframe, is the same argument now conducted about launch vehicles. Life-cycle cost analysis of the kind the argument needs appears in [Jung et al 2022][research_jung_2022], and the recovery and reuse literature cited below approaches the problem from the trajectory side. **The concept that the X-10 needed and did not have is the distinction between the cost of an airframe and the cost of a sortie**, and a programme that loses twelve of thirteen airframes has collapsed that distinction whether it meant to or not.

Current work makes the distinction explicit. Lifecycle cost estimation for a reusable launch vehicle with the critical parameters identified is [Du et al 2025][research_du_2025], recovery-method comparison across mission classes is [Lee et al 2026][research_lee_2026], mission-based optimisation of a reusable unmanned vehicle is [Jung et al 2026][research_jung_2026], precision landing guidance that makes recovery repeatable is [Chen et al 2026][research_chen_2026], and the weapon-system version of the same accounting is [Setiawan et al 2025][research_setiawan_2025]. **Whatever else such an accounting includes, it spreads the cost of an airframe over the flights that airframe makes**, so the number of flights per article governs it, and for the X-10 that number was 2.08.

### Automatic Landing Revisited

[Brukarczyk et al 2021][research_brukarczyk_2021] lands a fixed-wing unmanned aircraft automatically, reusable launch vehicle recovery trajectory planning appears in [Cheng et al 2021][research_cheng_2021] and [Mathavaraj and Padhi 2020][research_mathavaraj_padhi_2020], reusable landing structures are [Wang et al 2020][research_wang_2020_3], and landing gear efficiency and failure work is [Han et al 2019][research_han_2019] and [Diltemiz 2021][research_diltemiz_2021]. The X-10's loss record is a reminder that recovery is a distinct engineering problem from flight, and the reusable-launch-vehicle literature has rediscovered this at much greater cost. Carrier-based automatic landing is [Zhang et al 2025][research_zhang_2025_2], and the modern answer to the height-above-ground problem the X-10 had to solve with 1953 instrumentation is vision, in [Cheng and Lai 2026][research_cheng_lai_2026], [Han et al 2026][research_han_2026], and [Zhu et al 2026][research_zhu_2026].

### The Landing Gear and the Lost Fleet

Twelve of thirteen airframes were lost, and [North American X-10][ref_x10] puts six of the nine not expended deliberately down to landing accidents, which turned on chutes, barriers, and directional control. That subject has a current literature larger than the guidance one. Terminal manoeuvres including gear dynamics are [Cacciola and Calabria 2026][research_cacciola_calabria_2026], shimmy, which is the directional instability that takes a vehicle off a runway, is [Liu et al 2026][research_liu_2026], impact loads are [Liu et al 2023][research_liu_2023_2], structural design for ultimate load is [Titov and Serebryansky 2026][research_titov_serebryansky_2026] and [Chen and Chen 2026][research_chen_chen_2026], semi-active control of touchdown loads is [Durmuşoğlu 2026][research_durmusoglu_2026], and the failure side is [Xuan 2026][research_xuan_2026], [Sun et al 2024][research_sun_2024], [Chen et al 2022][research_chen_2022], and [Hsu et al 2022][research_hsu_2022] on predicting when a gear will fail before it does. **The X-10 had none of this and lost half of its fleet to it.** The loss record states plainly where the programme's engineering attention was not.

### Supersonic Inlets and Buzz Prediction

The inlet result that this article can only bound would today be resolved computationally. [Yamamoto et al 2020][research_yamamoto_2020] and [Farahani et al 2019][research_farahani_2019] predict buzz onset, [Chen and Tan 2019][research_chen_tan_2019] examines buzz diversity under strong disturbance, external-compression inlets free of violent buzz are [Chen et al 2019][research_chen_2019], suppression mechanisms are [Luo et al 2020][research_luo_2020], sideslip effects are [Dong et al 2019][research_dong_2019], and acoustic and vibration behaviour is [Zhu et al 2020][research_zhu_2020], with a recent experimental study in [Sepahi-Younsi 2025][research_sepahi_younsi_2025].

The failure modes that the X-10's designers could not name are now the subject matter. Unstart of the inlet and isolator is [Huang et al 2026][research_huang_2026], the shock-wave and boundary-layer interaction that drives it is [Kim and Park 2026][research_kim_park_2026], distortion delivered to the compressor is [Yang et al 2026][research_yang_2026_4] and [Bond and Key 2026][research_bond_key_2026], detection of distortion from measured signals is [Wang et al 2025][research_wang_2025_6], the diverterless arrangement that removes the boundary-layer splitter plate the X-10 needed is [Askari and Abedi 2026][research_askari_abedi_2026], and integrated airframe and propulsion control is [Zeng et al 2026][research_zeng_2026]. **The article's inlet inference, which had to be made from the vehicle's top speed because no full-scale duct measurement survives, is the kind of question a modern programme would answer by computation before the first article was built.**

### Coupled Aerothermal Analysis

The article puts the aluminium recovery-temperature limit at Mach 2.27 with a one-line relation and a representative recovery factor. A modern programme would compute it coupled to the structure. Aerothermoelastic analysis is [Kimmel et al 2026][research_kimmel_2026] and [Thawait et al 2024][research_thawait_2024], the coupled aerothermal calculation itself is [Bi et al 2024][research_bi_2024], thermal protection and drag reduction together are [Zuo et al 2025][research_zuo_2025], and optimisation across the aerothermal and structural problem at once is [İpek 2025][research_ipek_2025]. **The X-10 stopped just short of Mach 2.27 because it was made of aluminium, and the Navaho had to cross it. The accessible record gives no sign that the boundary was ever computed rather than met.**

### Parameter Identification From Flight Data

The X-10's task was to estimate parameters of a system from flight data, and that is now a discipline. Aerodynamic parameter identification from flight test spans [Cao and Wei 2020][research_cao_wei_2020], [Hui et al 2019][research_hui_2019], and [Kulhánek 2019][research_kulhanek_2019], with in-flight lift and drag estimation in [Bergmann et al 2021][research_bergmann_2021] and unmanned flight-test evaluation in [Arif and Sasongko 2021][research_arif_sasongko_2021]. **The identifiability calculation performed above is the standard first question of that discipline and it was not asked in 1953.** Here, more plainly than anywhere else, the article applies a later method to an earlier programme.

### Validation Across the Model-to-Flight Gap

The article establishes that the free-flight models reached between a fifth and a half of full-scale Reynolds number, and that the full-scale vehicle then flew above the highest Mach number either ground method had covered. Quantifying the confidence such an extrapolation deserves is now its own subject. Uncertainty quantification of aerodynamic prediction is [Eldredge and Mousavi 2026][research_eldredge_mousavi_2026], [Zhang et al 2025][research_zhang_2025_10], and [Li et al 2023][research_li_2023_4], the turbomachinery case is [Fu et al 2023][research_fu_2023], surrogate-model credibility is [Kirsch et al 2025][research_kirsch_2025], and computational drag estimation for configuration trade studies is [Jesudasan et al 2026][research_jesudasan_2026]. **A modern programme would attach a confidence interval to the extrapolation the X-10 programme made**, and the article's inability to say whether the sub-normal-shock duct recovery was real or an artefact of scale is the direct cost of that missing interval.

### Gravity Modelling From Orbit

The deflection-of-the-vertical term that dominates the budget above is now largely a solved problem, because the gravity field has been surveyed from orbit to a resolution the 1950s could not approach. Satellite gravimetry and the geoid models built from it are what removed the term, and the star-tracker calibration work of [Siemes et al 2019][research_siemes_2019] comes from the same mission family. **The single largest irreducible error in the Navaho's budget was eliminated not by a better instrument but by a better map**, a kind of progress the programme could not have anticipated or purchased.

The quantity the article computes is still being refined. A modern vertical-deflection dataset is [Schreutelkamp and Hirt 2026][research_schreutelkamp_hirt_2026], and optimising a deflection model from multidirectional data is [Li et al 2025][research_li_2025_6].

**The deeper inversion is that the error term has become a navigation aid.** Where the Navaho was defeated by not knowing the gravity field, a modern vehicle matches the field it measures against a stored map and fixes its position from the residual, which turns the article's dominant error source into an observation. Gravity-aided inertial navigation is [Ahmadian 2026][research_ahmadian_2026] and [Mao et al 2024][research_mao_2024], map matching against a gravity anomaly field is [Li et al 2026][research_li_2026_3] and [Li et al 2024][research_li_2024_4], the gradient-tensor version is [Wan et al 2025][research_wan_2025], [Li et al 2025][research_li_2025_5], and [Gao et al 2024][research_gao_2024], and measuring the anomaly from a moving vehicle in the first place is [Zhang et al 2024][research_zhang_2024_3].

### The Return of the Exposure Argument

The Navaho died because an airbreathing weapon is exposed for 172 minutes where a ballistic one is exposed for 32. That trade is live again, because the hypersonic glide vehicle is an attempt to get ballistic timelines with cruise-like manoeuvre, and the entire modern literature on tracking such a vehicle is an argument about how long the defender has.

Trajectory optimisation and manoeuvrability trade-offs for a glide vehicle are [Doronzo 2026][research_doronzo_2026] and [Bonavita et al 2026][research_bonavita_2026]. The defensive side, which is prediction of where such a body will be, is [Cai and Zhuang 2025][research_cai_zhuang_2025], [Li et al 2025][research_li_2025_4], [Zang et al 2025][research_zang_2025], [Jang and Park 2026][research_jang_park_2026], and [Ünal et al 2025][research_unal_2025], with the ballistic reference case in [Dudush and Snovydovych 2026][research_dudush_snovydovych_2026]. **The reason so much effort goes into predicting a glide trajectory is that manoeuvre destroys the closed-form prediction the article used to compute 32.2 minutes**, and a defender who cannot predict has no engagement timeline at all. The Navaho's argument here runs in reverse, which explains why the airbreathing option is being reconsidered rather than merely remembered.

### Command Links and Latency

The article computes a radio horizon of 482 kilometres against a thousand-kilometre leg, so a one-way X-10 leg of that length would have taken the vehicle beyond command range. Modern unmanned operations have the same constraint and a much larger literature on living with it. Multi-hop command and telemetry is [Miura 2022][research_miura_2022], and the human-factors consequence of a delayed link, which is that an operator cannot close a loop faster than the link allows, is [Cox and Wong 2019][research_cox_wong_2019] and [Moniruzzaman et al 2021][research_moniruzzaman_2021]. **The X-10's answer was to make the vehicle autonomous past the horizon**, and practice now arrives at the same answer, seventy years and a great deal of bandwidth later.

### Supersonic Cruise

Periodic cruise guidance for hypersonic vehicles is [Gao et al 2020][research_gao_2020], integrated guidance and control for morphing hypersonic missiles is [Bao et al 2019][research_bao_2019], and ascent trajectory design is [Zhai and Yang 2020][research_zhai_yang_2020]. The airbreathing intercontinental weapon did not return, but the airbreathing hypersonic weapon is being attempted again, and the exposure-time argument that killed the Navaho applies to it in modified form.

### Gyroscopes, accelerometers and the inertial instrument

**The instrument whose drift the X-10 was built to measure.** Gyroscopes of every mechanism, together with navigation accelerometers, their bias and drift, noise characterisation and temperature behaviour. **279 of these titles name a micro-electromechanical instrument and 230 a fibre-optic gyroscope**, against 20 that name a floated, electrostatic, superconducting, cryogenic or dynamically tuned instrument of the older kinds. 141 titles name temperature or thermal effects, and 81 of those compensate the drift that temperature causes, which is the modern answer to the platform oven computed above.

**The airframe the testbed was built to validate.** Canard configurations, missile aerodynamics, wave, base and transonic drag, the area rule and supersonic aircraft design. **154 titles name a canard**, from the NACA configuration studies of the 1950s to canard-controlled missiles and close-coupled canard fighters.

**The keystone, which is how a navigator's errors grow.** Error equations and their propagation, Schuler tuning and the damping of Schuler oscillation, the error budget of a navigation system, and the unstable vertical channel with its barometric aiding. **16 of these titles name Schuler**, and the record runs from the error equations of the period to error models for modern strapdown and rotating systems, which is the shift from bounding the error by hand to propagating it by machine that the review above describes.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

Treating the X-10 through its navigation keystone illuminates the programme's central failure but misleads in five ways, and they together are the strongest argument that the vehicle was mismatched to its job.

**It could not test the propulsion.** The Navaho cruised on ramjets. A ramjet has no compressor, so its pressure ratio is the ram ratio

$$\frac{p_{0}}{p_{\infty}} = \left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}}$$

which is exactly 1.000 at rest and therefore provides no cycle at all. **A ramjet cannot take off from a runway**, so a recoverable runway-operating testbed necessarily uses a different engine, and the X-10's two turbojets tested nothing about the Navaho's propulsion. Ramjet and turbojet cycle relations are in [Hill and Peterson 1991 Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Propulsion][book_hill_peterson_1991], and the engine the weapon needed was evaluated separately in [Reilly and Welna 1955][research_reilly_welna_1955].

**It could not test the boost phase.** The Navaho reached ramjet takeover on a liquid rocket booster, and the specific energy that booster had to supply is

$$e = \tfrac{1}{2} v^{2} + g h = \tfrac{1}{2} (818.9)^{2} + 9.80665 \times 24{,}000 = 0.571 \, \text{MJ/kg}$$

equivalent to an ideal velocity increment of 1068 metres per second. The X-10 took off under its own power and had no booster, so the entire boost and staging sequence, during which the first XSM-64 flight failed [Cleary 1991 The 6555th, The NAVAHO Program][ref_cleary_1991], was outside its scope.

**It could not test the structure.** The aluminium frontier at Mach 2.27 sits above the X-10's maximum of 2.05 and far below the Navaho's 3.25, so the testbed flew inside the material regime the weapon had to leave. What lay on the other side of that frontier was being worked out contemporaneously by [Chen 1958][research_chen_1958] and [Stauffer 1964][research_stauffer_1964], on structures the X-10 was never built to carry.

**It could not test the duration.** The Navaho had to navigate for 172 minutes, and the longest reported X-10 navigation flight lasted 79, or 0.46 of the mission. That flight was long enough to separate the drift from the accelerometer bias, but not to show that the drift held steady over the further hour and a half a Navaho mission required. Of the first four it is the least visible, because the other three show in the hardware while this one shows only in the clock.

**It could not test the environment the accuracy was claimed in.** The budget above shows the deflection of the vertical consuming most of the requirement, and every X-10 navigation flight was made over a surveyed range. A test that removes the dominant error term by choosing where to fly measures the instrument and not the mission. The size of the term being removed is what [Hagiwara 1972][research_hagiwara_1972] and [Talwani 1966][research_talwani_1966] establish.

Four of these five lie in the vehicle. The fifth lies in the test range, and only it could have been fixed without building a different aeroplane.

What the X-10 could and did test is the aerodynamic configuration, the autopilot, the airframe systems, and the practicality of recovering a large unmanned supersonic vehicle. That is a real and useful list. It is not the list of things that decided whether the Navaho worked.

## Is It an Aircraft, and Does the Question Have an Answer

The opening promised that the X-10 makes the not-an-aircraft framing hard to defend, and the material above is enough to settle what the difficulty is.

Every physical test fails. The X-10 had a wing, a tail, a fuselage, retractable landing gear, air-breathing engines, and a runway. It took off, cruised, manoeuvred, descended, and landed, repeatedly, and was maintained between flights by people who serviced it as they would have serviced an aeroplane. The [X-8][related_post_a305_aerojet_x8] had none of these properties and the [X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9] had some of them once per airframe. If the category is defined by what the object is, the X-10 is an aeroplane and the question is closed.

Every purpose test also fails, in the opposite direction. The X-10 existed to produce a number for a weapon programme. It carried no payload, served no transport function, and was expended when it stopped being useful, three of them, by the account of [North American X-10][ref_x10], deliberately flown into an island. **The property that makes it not an aircraft is that nothing aboard it was ever the point.**

What the article's analysis adds is that the two tests do not merely disagree, they interact. The vehicle's aircraft-like properties compromised its measurement. It was recoverable, so it needed turbojets, so it could not test the ramjet. It was recoverable, so it was built of aluminium, so it could not exceed Mach 2.27. It was recoverable, so every flight had to end on a runway, and runway landings consumed the fleet before it had completed more than a handful of navigator flights. **Every concession to being an aeroplane cost it something as an instrument**, and that trade is the most interesting thing about the vehicle.

The series has now met three consecutive designations that resist the research-aircraft model, and they resist it in three different ways. The X-8 was an instrument carrier that measured something other than itself. The X-9 was a weapon prototype that measured a control loop. The X-10 is a testbed whose form and whose function pulled against each other.

**Three exceptions with three distinct structures would not be a pattern. Three exceptions with one common origin are.** All three were RTV-A vehicles before they were X vehicles, and the Programme Origin section above records that two of them became X numbers in the same act of 1951 and that the date for the third is disputed. The right conclusion is therefore not that the X-series broadened to admit sounding rockets, missiles, and testbeds on their merits, but that a separate series was absorbed and its contents inherited the letter. Whether that absorption was ever a decision, as against a filing convenience, is the question the series' synthesis article has to answer, and the three cases now on the table are its evidence. The synthesis weighs the accumulated cases, and the X-10 contributes the sharpest single instance, because for this vehicle being an aeroplane was actively expensive.

## The Source Base

**The survey rests on 8,521 research records assembled from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,344 are report primaries, being 15.8 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The vehicle-specific record within it is small, and the topical record is large**, which is the shape of the evidence this section describes.

The accessible primary record for this vehicle is the thinnest of any article in this series so far, and the shape of the scarcity is more interesting than its extent.

**The vehicle is indexed under its project number, not its designation.** Queries against the aerospace archive for "X-10" and for "Navaho" return almost nothing usable, while "MX-770" returns [Pfyl 1952][research_pfyl_1952] and [Bond and Swanson 1953][research_bond_swanson_1953] immediately. A researcher who does not know the project number will conclude the record is empty when it is merely filed elsewhere. For this vehicle the right name within an archive matters as much as the right archive.

**The defence archive that holds project documents for the X-9 holds none for the X-10.** A Crossref search restricted to the Defense Technical Information Center publisher prefix on the project number MX-776 returns a report on the RASCAL weapon system, named for its radar scanning link, which is the [X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9] programme's own. The identical search on MX-770 returns nothing about the Navaho at all. Same archive, same query shape, adjacent project numbers, opposite results. **The gap is therefore a property of the record and not of the search.**

**Three documents in the accessible record concern the actual hardware.** They are [Pfyl 1952][research_pfyl_1952] on the 0.07-scale tunnel model, [Bond and Swanson 1953][research_bond_swanson_1953] on the 0.12-scale free-flight model, and [Church and Taylor 1959][research_church_taylor_1959] on a 0.05-scale model of the XSM-64A missile and booster, which is the weapon rather than the testbed. Everything else in this article's reference base is topical rather than vehicle-specific, drawn from the very large period literature on inertial navigation, canard aerodynamics, supersonic inlets, automatic landing, and flight test. Two further documents name the programme, a 1958 news item in Electrical Engineering reporting that an automatic landing system had landed the X-10 [Automatic landing system successfully 1958][ref_automatic_landing_1958], which is a notice rather than a research record, and a history of the Navaho's technology by [Myers 1992][research_myers_1992], and neither is a technical report on the configuration.

That distribution is what makes the article possible at all. The vehicle-specific record would support perhaps four hundred words. The topical record supports the analysis performed here, because the physics that governed the X-10 was being published in the open literature by the same laboratories at the same time, even when the vehicle itself was not.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when it is a NASA Technical Reports Server url or carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. The configuration reports on which the article's aerodynamic analysis rests are all reached through the reports server, so the rule counts them.

**The rule does not reach the journal and conference literature of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, abbreviated AIAA.** 1,937 of the records carry its 10.2514 prefix, among them 462 of the 965 records in the configuration cluster and 232 of the 482 in the inlet cluster. **15.8 percent is therefore a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.**

### Thin Subjects

**Eight subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the crossover between bounded accelerometer error and secular gyroscope drift | crossover time, dominant error | 1 |
| the length of the observation window in a navigation flight test | observation window, observation time, test duration, flight duration, duration of flight | 0 |
| temperature control of the inertial platform, the platform oven | temperature control, oven controlled, thermostat | 6 |
| the radio horizon of a command link | radio horizon, over the horizon, over horizon, beyond the horizon | 8 |
| recovery temperature and the service limit of aluminium | recovery temperature, adiabatic wall, aluminum alloy, aluminium alloy | 7 |
| flights per article as the measure of reuse | flights per, number of flights, turnaround, sortie | 0 |
| the dive onto the target and its angle sensitivity | dive phase, dive angle, dive bombing, diving | 4 |
| the Breguet range equation | breguet | 0 |

**The keystone construct is the thinnest of all.** One title names a dominant error source and none names the crossover time, against 281 records in the error propagation cluster. The bounded accelerometer term and the secular drift term are textbook results, so the papers propagate the full error model and the article's partition stands on the relations shown in The Research Question.

**No title names the length of the observation window**, which is the free variable of the article's design-of-experiments result. The discipline that would frame it is the experiment design cluster above, and none of its 335 records names the duration of a navigation test.

**The platform oven has become a compensation problem.** Six titles name temperature control of an inertial instrument, while 81 instrument titles compensate temperature-induced drift instead, so the oven the article treats as a first-order component now survives mostly as a model in software.

**The radio horizon and the aluminium limit are settled relations**, carried by a few propagation and materials titles, and the Breguet range equation is named by no title at all. **Flights per article, the parameter the reuse argument turns on, is named by no title**, so that argument stands on the X-10's own record.

### What the Survey Admits

**Every research title has been read for relevance, and a record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, which is the self-contained navigation of a long-range airbreathing missile, the recoverable supersonic testbed built to measure it, and the literatures the article's derivations and conclusions draw on. Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded. Navaho also names the Navajo people, their language and their crafts. Probable error is also a statistic of psychometrics and biometrics, and vertical deflection also names television deflection circuits and the bending of beams and pipes. Gravity wave drag belongs to atmospheric dynamics, and wave drag also to ships, piles and swimmers. Inertial also describes particle flows, reference frames and first-order lags. Identifiability, observability and experiment design are also the language of pharmacometrics, epidemiology, ecology, chemistry, economics and power systems. A flare is also a gas flare, stellar also names astrophysics, Doppler radar also names weather radar data assimilation, and the records of the White Sands Missile Range include its hydrology, geology and administration. Rotorcraft and vertical take-off aircraft, ships and underwater vehicles outside the field-matching literature, human motion sensing, ground robots, mining and drilling, satellite navigation in its own right, aircraft noise and emissions, and missile defence policy are excluded as outside the subject. Correction and retraction notices, unsigned news items, abstract-journal listings, encyclopedia volume titles and dictionary headwords are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are editorial events or parts of works. A review of a book, a reference or definition entry of two pages or fewer and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and are kept.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Gravity and magnetic map matching for underwater vehicles is kept because the field-matching literature is chiefly written for them and the article's gravity argument concerns the method. Star tracker work for spacecraft attitude is kept as the tracker's later history, lunar and planetary landing guidance and terrain-relative navigation as automatic landing and aided navigation elsewhere, and attitude control of reusable launch vehicles as the control of a recoverable flight vehicle. Several identifiability works from pharmacometrics, power systems and microalgae culture, a turbomachinery aerothermal calculation and turbomachinery uncertainty quantification, a quantum-computing study of aerothermal and structural optimisation for mobility systems, a vehicular optical communication link characterised by Allan variance, the flight test of a tilt-rotor unmanned aircraft, the landing gear of a quadrotor, and two underwater navigation studies are kept because the sentence citing each uses it for the method and not for the application. Teleoperation of ground vehicles under latency and land vehicle inertial navigation are kept for the same reason, because the article cites them for the latency of a command link and for aided inertial navigation. A reader may weigh each accordingly.

**The off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement rather than a sample estimate.**

## Epistemic State

**Historical fact, well supported.** The X-10 was the MX-770 testbed for the Navaho. Thirteen were built. The first flew on 14 October 1953 at Edwards. Fifteen flights were made at Edwards through March 1955 by five vehicles, and twelve more from Cape Canaveral between August 1955 and November 1956. The first Cape flight on 19 August 1955 ended with the vehicle overrunning the strip after its drag chute failed to deploy. A 200 by 10,000 foot strip was built at the Cape for the vehicle. Maximum demonstrated speed was Mach 2.05, given as 2.06 in the Air Force history. The Air Force cancelled the Navaho in July 1957, by a message dated 12 July in the Cape history, with 10 and 13 July given elsewhere. Two X-10s supported BOMARC tests on 24 September and 13 November 1958 and both burned after leaving the Skid Strip. The final flight was 26 January 1959. One vehicle survives.

**Historical fact, reported but from secondary compilations only.** The 1948 Air Force circular error probable requirement near 800 metres and the XN-1 drift near 1.6 kilometres per hour, both from a single web compilation, the accuracy goal of 1500 feet, which the Cape history gives as the goal of the weapon as a whole and not as a demonstrated stellar-inertial accuracy, and the count of five dedicated autonavigator flights, which the launch appendix of Werrell draws from the Air Force Systems Command index of missile launchings and of which the flight chronology describes four as navigation tests. **The first three figures carry the gyroscope-specification argument and none of them is traceable to a released programme document in the accessible record.** The requirement itself is stated differently across sources, as 800 metres in 1948 and 450 metres in 1950 in the web compilation, 1500 feet in the Cape history, and 12,000 feet after 5,000 miles, once relaxed, in the Air Force history. If those figures are wrong, the inverted gyroscope specifications are wrong by the same factor, though the structural conclusions about which error grows and which is bounded do not depend on them. The Edwards durations come from the launch appendix of Werrell and agree with the 32-minute first flight in the Air Force history. The Cape durations of 51, 62 and 79 minutes, the computer failures that aborted two navigator flights, and the flight-by-flight causes of loss rest on the single web compilation, and the appendix gives no Cape durations to check them against. **If the 79-minute figure is wrong, the finding that the navigation flight outlasted the crossover falls with it.** The sources also disagree about the N-6 itself, which the compilation calls stellar-inertial and the Air Force history all-inertial.

**Sources disagree and this article does not resolve it.** Reported X-10 length is 66 feet 2 inches in the designation history and 77 feet in other compilations, a difference of sixteen percent. Reported range is 1370 kilometres in one and 1009 kilometres in another. Reported service ceiling differs slightly between sources. The dimensions used in the calculations above are stated where they are used.

**Engineering analysis, derived here and independently checkable.** The Schuler frequency and period. The bounded form of the accelerometer error and the secular form of the gyroscope error. The crossover time of 47.8 minutes. The duration of 27.6 minutes for a thousand-kilometre leg at maximum Mach and its ratio of 0.58 to the crossover. The ratios of 1.07, 1.30 and 1.65 to the crossover for the reported Cape sorties of 51, 62 and 79 minutes, and the count of fourteen Edwards flights of fifteen below it. The exact orthogonality of the two error signatures over one Schuler period, proved by direct integration, the correlation of 0.974 over a maximum-speed leg with its variance inflation of 19.7, and the correlation of 0.140 over the 79-minute flight with its inflation of 1.02. The window-length sweep showing the optimum at exactly one Schuler period. The inverted gyroscope drift requirements. The star tracker inversions and the 17.1 minute refix interval. The azimuth equivalence of 2.9 kilometres per arcminute. The vertical-channel time constant of 570 seconds, its doubling time of 6.6 minutes, and the 18.1 e-foldings over a Navaho mission. The deflection-of-the-vertical contribution of 618 metres at ten arcseconds. The platform temperature control of 0.25 kelvin implied by the drift specification. The quadrature error budgets of 5617 metres pure inertial and 1488 metres stellar-inertial. The normal-shock and two-shock recovery figures. The radio horizon of 482 kilometres and its ratio of 2.08 to a thousand-kilometre leg. The turn radius of 21.5 kilometres at load factor two. The short-period frequency spread from 0.63 to 2.03 radians per second. The lift-to-drag ratio of 2.51, the reported mass ratio of 1.640, and the demonstration that the reported ranges are inconsistent with the reported weights on any cruise condition. The break-even inlet recovery of 0.622. The recovery temperatures and the Mach 2.27 aluminium frontier. The landing energy, stall speed, and braking distance. The statistical precision available from five flights and from three, and the mission-reliability product.

**Inference, argued but not established.** That the navigator's error was observed over the whole of the 79-minute flight, which the window calculation assumes. That the X-10's recoverability was motivated substantially by the statistical character of a drift measurement rather than by unit cost alone. That the free-flight duct recovery below normal-shock values reflects model scale and not the full-scale inlet, which the thrust-balance argument supports but does not prove, since it inherits the drag estimate. That any demonstration of the programme's accuracy goal was flown over surveyed range geometry and would not have transferred to unsurveyed territory. That the five testability gaps identified were understood at the time as gaps rather than accepted as adequate coverage. That the reported ranges describe a mission profile the article cannot reconstruct, the reported weights and the reported ranges being mutually inconsistent under every cruise assumption tried here.

**A budget that does not close is reported rather than reconciled.** The quadrature sum of representative error terms exceeds the programme's accuracy goal by a factor of 3.3, and the deflection-of-the-vertical term alone exceeds it. The article offers three readings and adopts none. It is the largest unresolved quantitative tension in the article, stated here and not smoothed.

**Assumptions made explicit.** An accelerometer bias of one ten-thousandth of a gravity, a subsonic minimum drag coefficient of 0.020, a span efficiency of 0.6, a landing mass of twelve tonnes, a maximum lift coefficient of unity, a braking friction coefficient of 0.4, a thrust specific fuel consumption of 1.0 per hour, a recovery factor of 0.89, a gyroscope temperature sensitivity of 0.01 degrees per hour per kelvin, a deflection of the vertical of ten arcseconds, a pitch inertia based on a radius of gyration of thirty percent of length, a mean chord inferred from area and aspect ratio, an effective Earth radius factor of four thirds for radio refraction, and the treatment of installed thrust as proportional to delivered total pressure. Each is representative rather than measured, and each is stated at the point of use so that a reader may substitute a better value.

**Where information postdates the editorial date.** The contemporary literature section is written from current knowledge.

## Out of Scope

The Navaho's booster engines and their descent into the Rocketdyne engine line, which deserve their own treatment and are the programme's largest legacy. The G-26 and G-38 vehicles as flight articles. The W-39 warhead. The Snark, the X-10's direct competitor, whose free-flight aerodynamic record is cited here only in passing. BOMARC, which appears only as the consumer of three surplus airframes. The detailed politics of the 1957 cancellation. The comparative economics of cruise against ballistic delivery, which is treated only to the depth needed to explain the cancellation. Digital computation, which arrived too late to matter to this vehicle.

## Conclusion

The X-10 was built to find out whether a machine could still know where it was after three hours of flight with nothing to look at but the stars. It was a good aeroplane. It flew to Mach 2.05, navigated across a range, and came home on its own wheels, a decade before airliners could land themselves. **It did not answer its question, and the record points to the number of its navigation flights more than to their length.**

The error a navigator accumulates from its accelerometers is bounded by the geometry of the planet at about 1.3 kilometres. The error it accumulates from its gyroscopes grows without limit. The two are equal at forty-eight minutes. A thousand-kilometre leg at the X-10's top speed would last twenty-eight, and over so short a window the two error signatures are ninety-seven percent correlated. The reported sorties were longer, however, and the one navigation flight whose duration is recorded lasted seventy-nine minutes, close to the eighty-four over which the two signatures are exactly uncorrelated. **For that flight the crossover argument does not hold**, and it holds only for the Edwards flights, which carried no navigator, and for a dash at top speed that no navigation flight is known to have been. What limited the measurement is that five autonavigator flights were made and two were aborted, which leaves the spread of the drift known to no better than about fifty percent, and that the longest of them lasted under half of the Navaho's three hours, over a surveyed test range.

Three of the series' vehicles have now been things other than aircraft, and the X-10 is the one that shows why the distinction is hard. It had wings, wheels, a runway, and a flight test programme. What it did not have was a pilot, and the consequence of not having a pilot was that its entire reason for existing was a measurement rather than a demonstration. **A demonstration succeeds by being performed once. A measurement of a spread succeeds only if it is repeated**, and a recoverable vehicle that kept destroying itself on landing could not be repeated often enough.
